candidate.title: Enter-key submit handler bypasses password-only approve-mode Accept-button gating, auto-authorizing unattended Android host connections without password check
candidate.component: flutter/lib/models/server_model.dart (Android CM login/voice-call dialog) + Rust ui_cm_interface::authorize sink
candidate.root_cause: showClientDialog() in server_model.dart conditionally renders the visible 'Accept' button only `if (approveMode != 'password')` (line 677-678), but unconditionally wires the SAME callback as `onSubmit: submit` on the underlying CustomAlertDialog (line 680, common.dart:1082). CustomAlertDialog's onKey handler (common.dart:1104-1109) fires `onSubmit?.call()` on ANY Enter/numpadEnter RawKeyDownEvent whenever `onSubmit != null`, with no re-check of approveMode. The button-hiding logic (the intended security gate that forces password-only hosts to reject click-approval) is therefore not enforced by the keyboard path, so `submit()` -> `onSubmit()` -> `sendLoginResponse(client, true)` -> `bind.cmLoginRes(connId, res:true)` runs even when the Accept button was never shown.
candidate.entry_point: Any Enter/numpadEnter key event delivered to the RustDesk Android CM app while a pending-connection ('Do you accept?') or incoming-voice-call dialog is on screen: a physical/Bluetooth keyboard attached to the Android host, an on-screen-keyboard 'Done/Go' action mapped to KEYCODE_ENTER, an accessibility-service/automation tool, or -- most relevant to the stated attack model -- a second, already-authorized malicious CONTROLLER session with keyboard/input permission on the same host synthesizing an Enter keypress that lands on the just-popped dialog for a second (colluding or same-attacker) connection attempt.
candidate.sink: flutter_ffi.rs::cm_login_res(conn_id, res=true) -> ui_cm_interface::authorize(id) (src/ui_cm_interface.rs:365-369, sets client.authorized=true and sends Data::Authorize) -> server/connection.rs Data::Authorize handler (line 676-685) -> conn.send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() -> full session authorization, WITHOUT ever calling validate_password().
candidate.attack: Attacker connects to a RustDesk Android host that is configured with Settings->Approve Mode = 'Accept sessions via password' (a legitimate hardening choice meant to remove the human-click gate and rely solely on password verification for unattended access). The connecting peer supplies no password (or a wrong one), causing the Rust side to call try_start_cm(..., authorized=false) and pop the 'Do you accept?' dialog with only a 'Dismiss' button visible (Accept intentionally hidden per approveMode=='password', server_page-equivalent logic at server_model.dart:677). Attacker then delivers an Enter keypress to the host's foreground app -- either directly (attached keyboard / automation) or via a second already-permitted RustDesk session's remote-keyboard-injection capability aimed at the just-opened dialog. CustomAlertDialog's onKey unconditionally invokes onSubmit, which calls sendLoginResponse(client, true) and cmLoginRes(res:true), authorizing the pending session with full 'Share screen'/remote-control access -- the exact outcome the password-only approve mode was configured to prevent.
candidate.trace: server_model.dart:610 showLoginDialog(client) -> server_model.dart:611-624 showClientDialog(..., onSubmit=()=>sendLoginResponse(client,true)) -> server_model.dart:643-684 builds CustomAlertDialog with actions:[Dismiss, if(approveMode!='password') Accept] but onSubmit: submit (line 680) always set -> common.dart:1063-1133 CustomAlertDialog.onKey (line 1104-1109) invokes onSubmit on Enter regardless of which action buttons were rendered -> server_model.dart:695-703 sendLoginResponse(client,true) calls bind.cmLoginRes(connId, res:true), sets client.authorized=true -> flutter_ffi.rs:2197-2204 cm_login_res -> ui_cm_interface.rs:365-369 authorize(id) sets CLIENTS[id].authorized=true, sends Data::Authorize -> server/connection.rs:676-685 Data::Authorize handler calls send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() which authorizes the session (connection.rs:1615-1654) without any password_security::validate_password call in this path.
candidate.preconditions: Android host (mobile CM UI, gated by `if (isAndroid...)` at server_model.dart:582/770). Approve Mode explicitly set to 'password' (Config option approve-mode='password', default is 'Both' per libs/hbb_common/src/password_security.rs:77-86, so this is an opt-in-hardened configuration, ironically the exact posture this bug most damages). Requires delivery of an Enter/numpadEnter RawKeyDownEvent to the CM UI while the dialog is shown -- feasible via attached keyboard, IME action key, accessibility automation, or (per the stated malicious-controller threat model) a second already-permitted session's keyboard-injection capability targeting the newly-opened dialog on the host's foreground.
candidate.confidence_reason: Code evidence is airtight for the Dart-side mismatch (button visibility vs onSubmit wiring) and the Rust-side sink (authorize() sets authorized=true with zero password re-validation) -- both confirmed by direct code reading, not inference. The same reused CustomAlertDialog pattern elsewhere in the file (showInputWarnAlert, showClientsMayNotBeChangedAlert, toggleService's dialogs) always keeps onSubmit consistent with the visibly-rendered submit button, reinforcing that the mismatch here is an oversight rather than intended behavior. Residual uncertainty is only about real-world delivery of the Enter keystroke to the correct foreground view on stock unrooted Android (soft-keyboard IME 'Enter' typically routes through TextInputAction rather than RawKeyEvent when no TextField has focus, and this dialog contains no TextField) -- a physical/Bluetooth keyboard or a second RustDesk session's own keystroke-injection channel are the most reliable delivery vectors and are plausible but not lab-verified here.
candidate.disposition_hint: needs-live-validation: verify on an actual Android RustDesk host (attach a Bluetooth keyboard or drive input via a second authorized RustDesk session's keyboard-injection) that pressing Enter while the password-approve-mode 'Do you accept?' dialog is showing indeed authorizes the pending connection; if confirmed, the fix is to gate `onSubmit` in showClientDialog on the same `approveMode != 'password'` condition used for the Accept button (or drop onSubmit entirely for showLoginDialog when in password mode).

verdict.reason: Code claims verified byte-for-byte and are accurate: server_model.dart:677-680 shows the Accept button is gated `if (approveMode != 'password')` but `onSubmit: submit` (line 680) is wired unconditionally; common.dart:1104-1109 (CustomAlertDialog.onKey) fires `onSubmit?.call()` on Enter/numpadEnter whenever `onSubmit != null`, with no re-check of approveMode or which buttons rendered — genuine gate/enforcement mismatch, not an inference. sendLoginResponse(true) -> flutter_ffi.rs:2197-2204 cm_login_res -> ui_cm_interface.rs:365-369 authorize() sets authorized=true and sends Data::Authorize -> connection.rs:676-685 handler calls send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() (connection.rs:1615-1657), which unconditionally sets self.authorized=true and even clears require_2fa (line 678) — zero password/2FA re-validation in this path, confirmed by direct reading. I also verified the Rust-side branch logic (connection.rs:2672-2748): when approve_mode==Password and the peer sends no/wrong password, try_start_cm(...,false) IS reached (lines 2715/2733), so the CM dialog really does pop in an unauthorized state for this config — the precondition holds. HOWEVER, the delivery/reachability claim needs correcting: I confirmed the attacker's OWN pending (self.authorized==false) connection cannot deliver this Enter keystroke itself — on_message only processes KeyEvent when `self.authorized` is already true (connection.rs:2835+), so the unauthorized peer's own input channel is closed. That leaves only: (a) a second, ALREADY-authorized session that was separately granted the 'keyboard' permission misusing that granted capability to inject Enter into the host's foreground CM dialog, (b) physical/Bluetooth keyboard attached to the host (local, not a remote bypass), or (c) host-side automation/accessibility tooling (implies host already compromised). Per the stated rating rule, a permission-gated action (keyboard-control) that a granted peer misuses to reach a security decision is rated LOWER than an ungated bypass — this is exactly that pattern, since the only credible remote vector requires the attacker to already hold a keyboard-permitted authorized session on the same host. Candidate's own confidence note already flags the on-screen-IME vector as weak (dialog has no TextField to route IME Enter through), leaving the keyboard-permission-misuse vector as the realistic one. The bug is real and does defeat the operator's password-only ('no click-approval') hardening plus bypasses 2FA when triggered, so it is not trivial — but rating it High/potential-Critical overstates it given the access precondition. Downgrading to Medium: real logic flaw, code-proven end-to-end, narrow to Android hosts in approve_mode='password', and its most credible trigger is a permission-gated misuse by an already-partially-trusted peer rather than an unauthenticated/ungated bypass.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Confirmed as stated: showClientDialog() hides the Accept button when approveMode=='password' (server_model.dart:677-678) but always wires the same submit() callback to CustomAlertDialog's onSubmit (line 680); CustomAlertDialog.onKey (common.dart:1098-1118) invokes onSubmit on any Enter/numpadEnter RawKeyDownEvent purely based on `onSubmit != null`, never re-checking approveMode or actions list, so the keyboard path is not covered by the same security gate as the button-visibility path. sendLoginResponse(true)->cmLoginRes->authorize() (ui_cm_interface.rs:365-369)->Data::Authorize (connection.rs:676-685)->send_logon_response_and_keep_alive() (connection.rs:1615-1657) contains no password_security::validate_password call, matching the candidate's claim exactly.
verdict.observed_mitigation: connection.rs:2835 gates KeyEvent/input-message processing on `self.authorized` being already true, so the pending/unauthorized connection whose own dialog is showing cannot deliver the Enter keystroke to itself — the attacker must already hold a separate, keyboard-permitted authorized session on the same host (permission-gated misuse) or have physical/BT-keyboard access to the host, both of which the task's rating rule places below an ungated bypass.
verdict.live_test: On a real Android RustDesk host with Approve Mode='password': (1) establish session A and grant it 'keyboard' permission; (2) from a second peer, initiate connection B without a valid password so the 'Do you accept?' CM dialog pops with only Dismiss visible; (3) from session A, use RustDesk's remote-keyboard-injection to send an Enter/KEYCODE_ENTER while the dialog is the foreground focused view; (4) observe whether connection B becomes authorized (client.authorized flips true, full session access granted) without any password check or human tap. Separately confirm whether Android's accessibility-based remote-input injection actually delivers a Flutter RawKeyDownEvent(logicalKey=enter) to the freshly-popped overlay dialog (vs. being swallowed by window-focus routing), since that specific plumbing detail cannot be confirmed from source alone.

candidate.root_cause: showVoiceCallDialog (line 632-641) reuses the same showClientDialog helper as showLoginDialog, inheriting the identical Accept-button-hidden-but-onSubmit-wired flaw (see primary finding). An Enter keypress accepts an incoming voice call from an unauthorized/unauthenticated peer even when host policy is password-only.
candidate.entry_point: Same as primary finding: Enter/numpadEnter key delivered to the CM UI while an incoming-voice-call dialog is shown.
candidate.sink: bind.cmHandleIncomingVoiceCall(id, accept:true) (server_model.dart:629) grants the peer an active voice channel without host click-confirmation.
candidate.attack: Peer initiates a voice call to the host; host's approveMode is 'password' so the Accept button is hidden per line 677, but Enter keypress (delivered the same way as the primary finding) still calls handleVoiceCall(client, true), starting the call.
candidate.trace: server_model.dart:632-641 showVoiceCallDialog -> showClientDialog(..., onSubmit=()=>handleVoiceCall(client,true)) -> same CustomAlertDialog onKey Enter path as primary finding -> server_model.dart:627-630 handleVoiceCall -> bind.cmHandleIncomingVoiceCall(accept:true).
candidate.preconditions: Same as primary finding (Android host, approveMode='password', Enter-key delivery to CM UI).
candidate.confidence_reason: Same code-level mechanism as the primary finding (shared helper), but the consequence (unwanted voice call) is far less severe than full remote-control authorization, and voice-call accept is arguably lower attacker value; grouped here as a secondary instance of the same root cause rather than an independent bug.
candidate.disposition_hint: Fold into the primary finding's fix -- gating onSubmit on approveMode in showClientDialog remediates both instances simultaneously.

verdict.reason: Code fully confirms the mechanism. common.dart:1098-1109 shows CustomAlertDialog's onKey handler calls onSubmit?.call() on Enter/numpadEnter unconditionally (no approveMode check) — the `if (approveMode != 'password')` guard at server_model.dart:677 only controls whether the Accept *button* is rendered, not the onSubmit wiring at line 680 (`onSubmit: submit`). showVoiceCallDialog (line 632-641) passes `() => handleVoiceCall(client, true)` as onSubmit, which calls bind.cmHandleIncomingVoiceCall(id, accept:true) → Rust ui_cm_interface.rs:1666 handle_incoming_voice_call() forwards Data::VoiceCallResponse(accept) to the connection with zero server-side re-check of approveMode — the accept/deny decision is 100% client-UI-decided. No mitigating layer exists anywhere in the chain; the candidate's trace is accurate line-for-line. However, the self-assigned severity (Medium, matching the primary login-bypass finding) is overstated relative to actual impact: (1) reaching this dialog requires the peer to already be an established/authorized client in server_model.dart's _clients list (updateVoiceCallState only fires showVoiceCallDialog for a client already present, index != -1) — i.e. this is a second-order abuse by a peer who has already cleared the connection gate, not a fresh compromise; (2) the consequence of the bypass is limited to opening a live two-way audio channel with the host operator (a privacy/nuisance primitive) — it grants no additional remote-control, file, keyboard, or data-exfiltration capability beyond what the peer's existing connection already has. That is materially lower attacker value than the primary finding's full unattended-control-session bypass, so it should not carry the same Medium rating.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Root cause is exactly as stated (shared showClientDialog helper decouples the visible Accept button from the always-wired onSubmit handler), but this is a secondary manifestation on an already-post-connection surface, not an independent authorization boundary.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None — no server/Rust-side re-validation of approveMode on VoiceCallResponse (ui_cm_interface.rs:1666-1671); confirmed as claimed, only severity is corrected.

candidate.title: Incoming host Clipboard sync is applied to the controller's OS clipboard without ever checking the host-granted 'clipboard' permission
candidate.root_cause: FfiModel.startEventListener's 'clipboard' branch in model.dart calls `Clipboard.setData(ClipboardData(text: evt['content']))` (line 365-366) unconditionally -- it never consults `ffiModel.permissions['clipboard']` (or any permission at all) before writing peer-supplied text into the local OS clipboard. Tracing the upstream Rust dispatcher confirms the same gap end-to-end: in src/client/io_loop.rs (~line 1463-1514) the `Some(message::Union::Clipboard(cb))` / `MultiClipboards` handlers gate application only on `clipboard_allowed = !lc.disable_clipboard.v && !lc.view_only.v` -- purely local controller-side toggles -- and never read `self.handler.server_clipboard_enabled` (the flag that mirrors the host-granted `Permission::Clipboard` state, set at io_loop.rs:1806 and surfaced to Dart via `set_permission('clipboard', ...)` -> FfiModel.updatePermission). By contrast, the OUTGOING (controller-to-host) direction correctly gates on this same flag via `SessionPermissionConfig::is_text_clipboard_required()` (src/ui_session_interface.rs:176-183: `*self.server_clipboard_enabled.read().unwrap() && ...`). This is a clear enforcement asymmetry: the 'clipboard' permission is checked before the controller SENDS its clipboard to the host, but never checked before the controller ACCEPTS and applies clipboard content sent BY the host.
candidate.entry_point: A malicious or compromised RustDesk HOST (the peer/machine being remotely controlled) sending a `message::Union::Clipboard` or `MultiClipboards` protobuf message at any point during an established session
candidate.sink: Clipboard.setData(...) in model.dart:365-366 (iOS, via the Dart event bridge) and, with the identical missing check, ClipboardContext::set() via update_clipboard()/do_update_clipboard_() in src/clipboard.rs (desktop platforms, direct Rust path bypassing Dart)
candidate.trace: malicious/compromised host sends Clipboard msg -> src/client/io_loop.rs ~1463 `Some(message::Union::Clipboard(cb))` -> `clipboard_allowed = !lc.disable_clipboard.v && !lc.view_only.v` (server_clipboard_enabled NOT checked) -> [iOS] self.handler.clipboard(content) -> src/flutter.rs:1055 push_event('clipboard', ...) -> model.dart FfiModel.startEventListener, evt['name']=='clipboard' (line 365) -> Clipboard.setData(...) overwrites the controller's system clipboard with attacker-chosen text, no permission re-check anywhere in the chain
candidate.attack: Attacker controls, or has compromised, the RustDesk HOST that a victim (e.g. an IT/support technician) is connected to as controller. At any time in the session -- including immediately on connect, or right after the host operator explicitly revokes 'clipboard' permission from the Connection Manager UI -- the malicious host process emits a Clipboard protobuf message containing a crafted string (e.g. a PowerShell/bash one-liner). The victim's own OS clipboard is silently overwritten. Paired with a social-engineering prompt via chat/msgbox ('paste this into a terminal/Run dialog to fix the session'), the victim later pastes and executes the attacker's payload on their own controller machine -- a pastejacking/ClickFix-style RCE pivot that flips RustDesk's usual trust direction (host attacking controller instead of controller attacking host).
candidate.preconditions: Any established session (default/remote-desktop connType); requires the controller to not have manually set disable_clipboard=true and to not be in view-only mode (both default to allowing sync); does NOT require the host to actually have been granted 'clipboard' permission at the protocol level, since server_clipboard_enabled is tracked but never read on the receive path; reachable on Windows/macOS/Linux via the direct Rust clipboard write and on iOS via the model.dart Dart sink
candidate.confidence_reason: Confirmed via full static cross-file trace (Dart sink in model.dart + Rust dispatch in io_loop.rs/ui_session_interface.rs/flutter.rs/clipboard.rs): server_clipboard_enabled is set on Permission::Clipboard receipt and IS consulted for the outgoing direction (is_text_clipboard_required) but is provably absent from the incoming Clipboard/MultiClipboards handler and from the Dart sink. Not yet live-validated against a running host/controller pair, so the runtime behavior (e.g. whether a legitimate host's own capture loop would ever emit a message in this state) has not been dynamically confirmed.
candidate.disposition_hint: validate: stand up host+controller instances (lab), toggle 'clipboard' permission off from the CM UI mid-session, then use an instrumented/modified host build (or direct protobuf injection) to send a Clipboard message and confirm the controller's OS clipboard still updates despite the revoked permission; also verify behavior on iOS specifically since that is the only platform where the Dart sink in model.dart is reachable.

verdict.reason:
Directly re-read every hop in the chain and the asymmetry is real and provable, not inferred.

(1) model.dart:365-366 — the 'clipboard' branch of FfiModel.startEventListener calls `Clipboard.setData(ClipboardData(text: evt['content']))` unconditionally. A grep across the entire flutter/lib tree confirms `_permissions['clipboard']` is written by updatePermission() but never READ anywhere in Dart (contrast with `keyboard`, which has a live getter at model.dart:250 consulted elsewhere) — so there is no permission gate on the Dart side.

(2) src/client/io_loop.rs:1461-1465 and :1490-1494 — both `Some(message::Union::Clipboard(cb))` and `Some(message::Union::MultiClipboards(_mcb))` compute `clipboard_allowed = !lc.disable_clipboard.v && !lc.view_only.v` (a purely local controller-side toggle), and this is the ONLY gate before the iOS branch calls `self.handler.clipboard(content)` (-> flutter.rs:1054 push_event -> Dart sink) or the desktop branch calls `update_clipboard()` (verified no permission check inside update_clipboard_/do_update_clipboard_ in src/clipboard.rs either). `server_clipboard_enabled` is never referenced in either receive handler.

(3) By contrast the OUTGOING direction is properly gated: src/ui_session_interface.rs:178-182 `is_text_clipboard_required()` explicitly ANDs in `*self.server_clipboard_enabled.read().unwrap()`, which src/client.rs's ClientClipboardHandler polls before the controller sends its own clipboard to the host.

(4) `server_clipboard_enabled` is confirmed to mirror the host-granted permission: set at io_loop.rs:1806 exactly on `Ok(Permission::Clipboard) => *self.handler.server_clipboard_enabled.write().unwrap() = p.enabled`, alongside `self.handler.set_permission("clipboard", p.enabled)` — the same call that populates the (unused-for-gating) Dart permissions map.

This is a genuinely UNGATED receive path, not a case of "a granted peer misusing a permission it holds" (which the task's rubric marks lower) — the check is simply absent regardless of grant state, matching the candidate's own framing. The candidate's Medium/potential-High self-rating is already well-calibrated: it correctly discounts to Medium because converting the clipboard write into code execution still requires a second, independent step (the victim must be socially engineered into pasting attacker content into their own shell/Run dialog; RustDesk has no host->controller keystroke-injection primitive to auto-trigger paste+execute). No severity correction warranted.

candidate.title: Attacker-controlled remote file name overrides file-transfer download destination -> arbitrary absolute-path file write on the controller's machine
candidate.root_cause: sendFiles() in file_model.dart computes the local download destination as `to: PathUtil.join(toPath, from.name, isWindows)` (line 596) where `from.name` is the unsanitized `Entry.name` taken verbatim from the remote peer's directory-listing JSON (`Entry.fromJson`, line 1583: `name = json['name'];`, no validation at all -- contrast with `PathUtil.validName()` which IS applied to locally-typed rename/create-folder input at lines 882 and (mobile/desktop file_manager_page.dart) but is never applied to remote-supplied names). `PathUtil.join` (lines 1771-1774) is a thin wrapper over Dart's `package:path` `Context.join()`, which (a) does not strip or reject `..` segments and (b) discards every preceding path component when a later argument is an absolute path. This lets a malicious remote entry name either traverse out of the user-selected download folder or fully replace it with an attacker-chosen absolute path.
candidate.entry_point: Malicious/MITM file-transfer remote peer's ReadDir response: an `Entry` (`entry_type`, `name`, `size`) inside the JSON payload consumed by `receiveFileDir()` (line 104) -> `FileDirectory.fromJson` (line 1542) -> `Entry.fromJson` (line 1580-1585).
candidate.sink: Rust client core, src/client/io_loop.rs, `Data::SendFiles` handler (~line 598-619): `let to = fs::DataSource::FilePath(PathBuf::from(&to));` (line 604) feeding `fs::TransferJob::new_write(...)`. libs/hbb_common/src/fs.rs `TransferJob::write()` (line 759) then does `join_validated_path(p, &entry.name)` where `p` IS the poisoned `to`/base -- and `validate_transfer_file_names()` (fs.rs line 490-495) explicitly documents/allows an EMPTY relative name for single-file transfers 'because the destination file path is carried by transfer metadata', so for the overwhelmingly common single-file download the base path is used completely unvalidated and `File::create(&path)` (fs.rs line 798) writes straight to it.
candidate.trace: file_model.dart receiveFileDir() [104] -> FileDirectory.fromJson [1542] -> Entry.fromJson name=json['name'] [1583, unsanitized] -> FileDirectory.format(): entry.path = PathUtil.join(path, entry.name, isWindows) [1553] -> user selects entry -> FileController.sendFiles(items, otherSideData) [570] -> to = PathUtil.join(toPath, from.name, isWindows) [596] -> bind.sessionSendFiles(..., to: to, isRemote: true) -> src/flutter_ffi.rs session_send_files -> session.send_files(...) -> src/client/io_loop.rs Data::SendFiles handler: to=PathBuf::from(&to) [604] -> fs::TransferJob::new_write(...) [609] (write_jobs) -> on receipt of file bytes, TransferJob::write() [fs.rs 759] resolves path via join_validated_path(p=to, entry.name) [fs.rs 779] where entry.name is empty for the common single-file case (fs.rs 490-495 comment) -> File::create(&path) [fs.rs 798] writes verbatim to the attacker-influenced path.
candidate.attack: Attacker runs (or MITMs) the RustDesk host the victim connects to for file transfer. When the victim's client sends a ReadDir request, the attacker's server replies with a directory entry, e.g. entry_type=file, name='../../../../home/victim/.ssh/authorized_keys' (POSIX relative-traversal) or name='/home/victim/.bashrc' / on Windows name='C:\\Users\\victim\\AppData\\Roaming\\Microsoft\\Windows\\Start Menu\\Programs\\Startup\\evil.exe' (absolute-path override, which fully discards the victim's chosen download folder per Dart path.join semantics). The victim, browsing the file manager, selects that entry (or clicks 'select all' / downloads a folder containing it) and presses Download. The client silently writes the attacker-supplied file content to that exact path on the victim's own machine (no dialog warns about the destination, since it's assumed to be inside the visibly-chosen local folder) -> attacker plants an SSH authorized_keys entry / cron.d job / systemd user unit / Windows Startup executable -> code execution on the victim's machine on next login/cron tick/reboot.
candidate.preconditions: Victim has an active file-transfer connection to an attacker-controlled or MITM'd RustDesk peer and downloads at least one entry from that peer's file listing. No special permission is required on the attacker side beyond being the file-transfer peer -- this is a client-side path-construction bug with zero server(host)-side re-validation for the single-file-transfer case (explicitly documented as trusted metadata in libs/hbb_common/src/fs.rs).
candidate.confidence_reason: Traced end-to-end in the actual checked-out source: confirmed Entry.name is unsanitized in file_model.dart, confirmed PathUtil.join's absolute-override/no-'..'-stripping semantics match Dart's package:path join() documented behavior, and confirmed on the Rust sink side (libs/hbb_common/src/fs.rs) that single-file transfers explicitly trust the destination-metadata path with zero validation (comment + `set_files_allows_single_empty_name_for_single_file_transfer` test name corroborate this is intentional, known-quantity trust boundary). Residual uncertainty: did not execute a live PoC, and did not verify whether any newer overwrite-confirmation dialog or UI-level name sanitization intercepts obviously-malicious display names before the user can select them.
candidate.disposition_hint: high-priority-verify

verdict.reason:
Every link in the chain was re-verified against the actual checked-out source (targets/rustdesk, commit 137298e) and holds up; no mitigating layer exists.

1. flutter/lib/models/file_model.dart:1583-1584 — `Entry.fromJson`: `name = json['name'];` — zero validation on the remote-peer-supplied directory-entry name. Confirmed by grep: `PathUtil.validName()` is called ONLY from local rename/create-folder text-input flows (file_model.dart:882, desktop/mobile file_manager_page.dart rename dialogs) — never from `Entry.fromJson` or anywhere in the receive-listing path.
2. file_model.dart:596 — `FileController.sendFiles`: `to: PathUtil.join(toPath, from.name, isWindows)` — confirmed verbatim at that line.
3. file_model.dart:1771-1774 — `PathUtil.join` is a bare passthrough to `package:path` `Context.join()` (pubspec.yaml: `path: ^1.8.1`), which does not strip `..` segments and discards preceding args when a later one is absolute — standard, well-documented behavior of that package.
4. src/client/io_loop.rs:602-616 — `Data::SendFiles` `is_remote=true` branch: `to = fs::DataSource::FilePath(PathBuf::from(&to))` then `TransferJob::new_write(..., to, ...)` — the Dart-poisoned string becomes the job's `data_source` base with no interposed check.
5. libs/hbb_common/src/fs.rs:490-495 — `validate_transfer_file_names`: explicitly allows an empty `FileEntry.name` for single-file transfers, with a comment stating the destination is "carried by transfer metadata" (i.e., by the base, not the name). Test name at fs.rs:1659 (`set_files_allows_single_empty_name_for_single_file_transfer`) corroborates this is intentional design, not an oversight in that specific function.
6. fs.rs:646-655 (`set_files`) and fs.rs:779 (`write()`) — the traversal/symlink checks (`validate_file_name_no_traversal`, `validate_no_symlink_components`, `join_validated_path`) are applied only to `entry.name`, never to the `base`/`to` (`DataSource::FilePath`) itself.
7. fs.rs:831-836 — `TransferJob::join(p, name)`: when `name` is empty (guaranteed for single-file transfers) it returns `p.clone()` unmodified — i.e., the final write path is exactly the attacker-tainted `to` string, byte for byte, with File::create writing straight to it (fs.rs ~798).

No barrier intercepts this: the UI renders `entry.name` raw (desktop/pages/file_manager_page.dart:1204, `Text(entry.name.nonBreaking, ...)`) with no filtering that would block selection/download of a traversal- or absolute-path-shaped name, and no destination-confirmation dialog gates the write. The Rust-side hardening added for `entry.name` traversal is real but structurally cannot fire on the single-file-download path because that field is empty by design — exactly as the candidate described. Directory downloads leak a related but slightly weaker primitive (poisoned base directory, inner names still individually traversal-checked).

verdict.reason:
The core claim is real and directly confirmed by code: InputModel.scroll() (input_model.dart:1100-1106) only checks `isViewCamera`, unlike sibling inputKey() (line 1030: `if (!keyboardPerm) return;`) and sendMouse() (line 1133: same check). I traced the full path end-to-end on both host platforms to resolve the ambiguity the candidate flagged in confidence_reason.

Desktop hosts: neutralized. session_send_mouse (flutter_ffi.rs:1921) builds a MouseEvent (mask=MOUSE_TYPE_WHEEL) that server-side connection.rs dispatches through `Some(message::Union::MouseEvent(mut me))` (line 2841); on non-android/non-ios targets this hits `if self.peer_keyboard_enabled()` (line 2850, which checks `self.keyboard && !self.disable_keyboard` — the server-side mirror of Dart's keyboardPerm) before calling input_mouse. So on Windows/Mac/Linux hosts the missing client-side check is fully compensated server-side, as the candidate speculated.

Android hosts: NOT neutralized, confirmed exploitable. The same MouseEvent match arm has a `#[cfg(any(target_os = "android", target_os = "ios"))]` branch (line 2845-2848) that calls `call_main_service_pointer_input("mouse", me.mask, ...)` UNCONDITIONALLY, before and independent of the peer_keyboard_enabled() gate (that gate is scoped `#[cfg(not(any(android, ios)))]`). Following this into the Android JNI target: MainService.kt `rustPointerInput()` (line 67) calls `InputService.ctx?.onMouseInput(mask, x, y)` with zero permission check, and InputService.kt onMouseInput handles WHEEL_UP/WHEEL_DOWN masks (lines 187-220) by synthesizing real swipe gestures via AccessibilityService.dispatchGesture — i.e. it actually scrolls the remote Android screen. No layer between the Dart call and the Android gesture dispatch re-checks keyboard/control permission. The server relies entirely on client-side gating for Android hosts, and scroll() is the one function missing it.

Correction to the candidate's entry-point claim: the three-finger-drag path it names does NOT work against Android hosts — remote_input.dart line 517 explicitly sets `onThreeFingerVerticalDragUpdate = ffi.ffiModel.isPeerAndroid ? null : (d){...}`, disabling that gesture for Android peers. However the OTHER entry point the candidate also cited, the floating-mouse-wheel widgets (floating_mouse.dart:567, floating_mouse_widgets.dart:343/346), carry no isPeerAndroid or permission gating anywhere in their call chain and render for any peer type based only on a UI touchMode toggle (mobile/pages/remote_page.dart:706, itself ungated) — so the bypass IS reachable, via the floating mouse wheel control, specifically against Android-hosted peers.

verdict.live_test: Not executed — verdict rests on a complete static trace across Dart client -> flutter_ffi.rs -> connection.rs -> JNI -> Kotlin MainService/InputService, with no remaining unobserved layer. UAC elevation-on-consent is an OS-level capability available to any code already running as the interactive user, not a boundary RustDesk's bug uniquely breaches. verdict.corrected_root_cause: Real code defect (missing shell-metacharacter/quote escaping when building the install .bat) confirmed by direct source reading, but not attacker-reachable through any lower-privilege interface: the sole legitimate caller constrains `path` to values returned by the native Windows folder picker, which cannot contain the `"` character required to break out of the quoted context, and no other caller passes untrusted path data. candidate.title: Privacy Mode is enforced only by a one-shot client-cooperative notice — other subscribed viewers keep receiving the real, unblanked desktop
candidate.root_cause: check_privacy_mode_changed() in video_service.rs detects a privacy_mode_id transition and only (a) sends every OTHER subscriber a single, best-effort Misc/BackNotification(PrivacyModeState::PrvOnByOther) message asking them to self-disconnect, and (b) restarts the shared per-display capturer so it now produces the privacy-mode owner's unblanked view. It never removes the other connections from the GenericService subscriber set (ServiceTmpl::subscribes), and because the check only fires on the edge (ci.privacy_mode_id != privacy_mode_id_2), the notice is sent exactly once per transition — there is no periodic re-check or forced disconnect if the peer ignores it. Every subsequent frame the shared capturer produces is broadcast unconditionally to all subscribers via handle_one_frame() -> sp.send_video_frame(msg) (video_service.rs:1172) -> ServiceTmpl::send_video_frame_shared() (service.rs:235) -> ConnInner::send() (connection.rs:422), which forwards to the socket with no privacy-mode filtering at all. On Windows, the frames the shared capturer produces once privacy mode is on are deliberately the REAL desktop: win_mag::create_capturer() (src/privacy_mode/win_mag.rs) uses CapturerMag::exclude(...) to capture 'under' the black overlay window, and the modern default implementation win_exclude_from_capture (src/privacy_mode/win_exclude_from_capture.rs, selected whenever SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE) is supported, i.e. Windows 10 2004+/11) marks the overlay window invisible to ALL capture APIs system-wide — including RustDesk's own regular DXGI/GDI capturer used for every subscriber, not just the activating connection.
candidate.entry_point: A second, already permission-accepted remote-control connection to the same host (malicious or custom-patched RustDesk client) that stays subscribed to the display's video_service instance.
candidate.sink: ConnInner::send() in src/server/connection.rs:422, reached via GenericService::send_video_frame_shared() in src/server/service.rs:235, called from handle_one_frame() in src/server/video_service.rs:1172 — forwards every captured frame to every subscribed connection unconditionally.
candidate.trace: TogglePrivacyMode misc message (connection.rs:3457) -> Connection::toggle_privacy_mode()/turn_on_privacy() (connection.rs:4301,4648) sets the global PRIVACY_MODE_CONN_ID -> next video_service run() loop iteration calls check_privacy_mode_changed() (video_service.rs:701-703, 1115-1134) which detects the ID change, sends the one-shot PrvOnByOther notice to other subscribers (line 1127), then bail!("SWITCH") -> capturer recreated via get_capturer_monitor()/create_capturer() (video_service.rs:391-483, 262-311) now bound to the new privacy_mode_id -> subsequent frames captured 'through' the excluded/magnifier-bypassed overlay -> handle_one_frame() -> sp.send_video_frame(msg) -> ServiceTmpl::send_video_frame_shared() iterates ALL subscribers (service.rs:235-243) -> ConnInner::send() (connection.rs:422) transmits to every socket, including the connection that never honored PrvOnByOther.
candidate.attack: Attacker holds (or opens) a second, ordinary permission-accepted Remote session to a host that allows multiple simultaneous connections (default unless the operator restricts to one connection). When the primary controller — or the attacker from their first session — enables Privacy Mode (TogglePrivacyMode), the server sends the attacker's second session exactly one PrivacyModeState::PrvOnByOther message and expects the RustDesk client to call `return false` in handle_back_msg_privacy_mode() (src/client/io_loop.rs:2263) and disconnect. The attacker runs a trivially patched open-source client that simply ignores/no-ops this one message type instead of disconnecting. The server never checks again and never force-closes that connection; it keeps receiving every subsequent VideoFrame from the display's video_service, which — due to the overlay being excluded from capture on Windows — shows the real, un-blanked desktop that Privacy Mode was supposed to hide from every viewer except the activating connection.
candidate.confidence_reason: The subscriber-broadcast model, the edge-triggered/one-shot PrvOnByOther notice, the unconditional ConnInner::send forwarding, and both Windows privacy-capture implementations bypassing the overlay for the shared capturer were all confirmed by direct code reading across video_service.rs, service.rs, connection.rs, privacy_mode.rs, win_mag.rs, win_topmost_window.rs, win_exclude_from_capture.rs, and client/io_loop.rs. Not yet dynamically reproduced (would need a Windows host with Privacy Mode licensed/enabled plus two live simultaneous connections, one running a client build that ignores PrvOnByOther) to visually confirm the second viewer keeps seeing real content rather than some other fallback blanking I haven't found in code.
candidate.disposition_hint: validate — set up a Windows lab host with Privacy Mode enabled, connect with two clients (patch client B's io_loop.rs PrvOnByOther arm to `return true` instead of `return false`), enable Privacy Mode from client A, and confirm client B continues receiving non-blank video frames instead of being disconnected.

verdict.reason:
Re-derived from raw source, every link in the chain checks out and no mitigating layer exists:

1. check_privacy_mode_changed (video_service.rs:1115-1134): on a privacy_mode_id transition it calls sp.send_to_others(msg_out, privacy_mode_id_2) exactly once (edge-triggered, no periodic re-check, no server-side forced disconnect anywhere in connection.rs — grepped for close/kick/disconnect near "privacy", zero hits).

2. send_to_others (service.rs:214-220) / send_video_frame_shared (service.rs:235-243): the video-frame broadcast path iterates ALL entries in `subscribes` unconditionally — there is no privacy-state check, no removal of the non-cooperating subscriber from the map.

3. ConnInner::send (connection.rs:414-436): confirmed no privacy-mode filtering whatsoever — it only picks tx vs tx_video channel by message type, then forwards.

4. Client-side handling (io_loop.rs:2256-2267, called from handle_back_notification at 1871-1880): PrvOnByOther causes the CLIENT to `return false`, which breaks its own read loop — i.e., the disconnect is a voluntary client-side action, not something the server can compel. A patched/custom client that ignores this one message simply keeps its socket open and keeps receiving frames.

5. Shared capturer: create_capturer() (video_service.rs:262-311) is one Boxed capturer per display/video_service instance, used for the whole broadcast loop. Whenever privacy_mode_id > 0 it unconditionally routes through win_mag::create_capturer() -> CapturerMag::exclude("", PRIVACY_WINDOW_NAME) (win_mag.rs) — this is the SAME magnifier-bypass technique used for ALL Windows privacy-mode impls (mag / topmost_window / exclude_from_capture all share this create_capturer path), and it produces a real, essentially-unblanked capture (only the black overlay window's own pixels are excluded). That capture is what gets broadcast to every subscriber via step 2.

One inaccuracy in the write-up: the specific citation of `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)` inside win_exclude_from_capture.rs is not literally present in this Rust source tree — that file only gates support via Windows-build-version check and reuses win_topmost_window's overlay-window logic; the actual window-affinity/injection mechanics live in the external WindowInjection.dll, which isn't in-repo. This doesn't undermine the finding: the confirmed win_mag capture-bypass path (used universally by create_capturer whenever privacy_mode_id>0) already fully establishes that the shared capturer feeds the real desktop to every subscriber, independent of which overlay impl is drawing the black screen.

Net: privacy mode's protection against a second, already-permission-accepted, simultaneously-subscribed viewer is enforced purely by a one-shot advisory notice + voluntary client self-disconnect, with zero server-side enforcement (no re-check, no forced close, no per-subscriber frame filtering). This is architecturally exactly as the candidate describes and is provable by static reading alone — no unobserved layer needs to be assumed insecure.

Per the grading rule that a permission-gated action a granted peer misuses rates lower than an ungated one — the attacker here must already hold accepted remote-control access via a second live connection and must run a client build that ignores one message type — the candidate's own Medium/High(potential) split is the correct calibration and I'm not adjusting it.
verdict.live_test: Not required to confirm the code-level flaw (fully provable statically), but for real-world impact confirmation: Windows lab host with Privacy Mode enabled + two simultaneous accepted connections (client A = stock, client B = patched to `return true` instead of `return false` in the PrvOnByOther arm of handle_back_msg_privacy_mode, io_loop.rs:2263). Toggle privacy mode from A, confirm B keeps rendering live, non-blank frames instead of disconnecting.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found — grepped connection.rs and service.rs for any close/kick/unsubscribe/disconnect logic tied to privacy-mode transitions; only hit is the one-shot notice at video_service.rs:1127. Confirmed the video-frame broadcast (service.rs:235) and ConnInner::send (connection.rs:422) are both privacy-mode-agnostic.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Same as candidate's root_cause, with one factual correction: drop/soften the specific `SetWindowDisplayAffinity(WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE)` citation for win_exclude_from_capture.rs — that mechanism is not present in the visible Rust source (it's gated by a Windows-build check and reuses win_topmost_window's overlay logic; the actual affinity/injection work happens in the out-of-tree WindowInjection.dll). The universally-confirmed mechanism is win_mag::create_capturer()'s CapturerMag::exclude(), which create_capturer() (video_service.rs:262-311) routes through for ANY active Windows privacy-mode impl whenever privacy_mode_id > 0 — that alone fully establishes the shared-capturer-produces-real-desktop claim.

verdict.reason:
Re-read dbus.rs line-by-line plus the two files it depends on for exploitability (core_main.rs, flutter/lib/common.dart, flutter/lib/models/model.dart). The mechanics claimed are all directly observable and confirmed:

1. dbus.rs:58 — `let _ = conn.request_name(DBUS_NAME, false, true, false)?;` discards the `RequestNameReply`. Per the D-Bus RequestName wire protocol (standard, not app-specific), with `replace_existing=true, do_not_queue=false`, this call essentially never returns `Err` on an ownership conflict — it silently returns `Ok(InQueue)` if another process already owns/refuses-replacement of `org.rustdesk.rustdesk`. The `?` only catches genuine bus-connection failures, so it does NOT act as an implicit ownership check. `start_dbus_server()` then unconditionally calls `cr.serve(&conn)` regardless of which reply variant came back. This confirms the name-squat race is real and unguarded.
2. dbus.rs:66-92 — `handle_client_message`'s closure signature `move |_, _, (_uni_links,): (String,)|` discards the `dbus_crossroads::Context` (arg 1), which is exactly the object that exposes the caller's D-Bus sender (`ctx.message().sender()`). No caller-identity check exists anywhere in the method. Confirmed no code path elsewhere adds one — module is `#[cfg(target_os = "linux")]` only (server.rs:52), started unconditionally by `main_start_dbus_server()` (flutter_ffi.rs:1842-1850) on every Linux flutter build, no `dbus`-scoped Cargo feature gate, no shipped D-Bus policy XML restricting the session-bus name (only `res/rustdesk.service`, a root systemd unit for the unrelated `--service` daemon on the *system* bus — irrelevant to this session-bus code path).
3. core_main.rs:807-860 confirms the full credential-embedding chain: a second `rustdesk --connect <id> --password <pass>` invocation (the real-world trigger is RustDesk's own "one-click support link" `rustdesk://connection/id?password=...` deep-link feature) builds `uni_links` containing literal `password=<pass>` and routes it via `try_send_by_dbus` → `invoke_new_connection` (dbus.rs:38-49) to whatever process currently owns the well-known bus name. flutter/lib/models/model.dart:420-422 → common.dart:2264 `handleUriLink()` confirms the receiving side parses `--password` and feeds it straight into `rustDeskWinManager.newRemoteDesktop/newFileTransfer/...`.

So the code defects (unchecked RequestNameReply, no sender check, plaintext password over this exact channel) are all provable from the source as claimed — no refuting mitigation exists in the cited functions or in Cargo.toml gating.

What is mis-rated is the severity/threat-model framing. `Connection::new_session()` (dbus.rs:57) is the per-user SESSION bus, not the system bus used by the root `rustdesk.service` — so the "attacker" in this scenario is already a co-resident process running as the SAME OS user as the victim's RustDesk GUI. No privilege boundary is crossed (attacker doesn't go from unprivileged→privileged, or user→root/SYSTEM), so this doesn't actually fit the 'LOCAL attacker (privesc via IPC/driver/service)' bucket the candidate invokes — it's same-privilege IPC abuse, not privilege escalation. Exposing an unauthenticated method on the session bus is also a widespread, largely-accepted Linux desktop IPC pattern precisely because the session bus itself is the trust boundary (same UID = already trusted) — a mitigating design factor, though not a full refutation since the leaked asset here (a plaintext password to a *different*, remote system) is a genuine cross-domain credential exposure, not merely local self-harm. Sub-case (a) (spoofed deep link) mostly just forces the victim's GUI to open an attacker-chosen outbound connection — low incremental value to an attacker who already has local code execution as that user. Sub-case (b) (credential interception) is the more serious half, but is gated by a login/startup timing race (attacker must squat the name before/while the legitimate instance starts) and only fires for the non-default `--connect/--password` deep-link workflow, not the normal GUI-typed-password flow.
verdict.corrected_root_cause: Confirmed as coded: (1) start_dbus_server() ignores the RequestNameReply, so it proceeds to serve even when it lost the well-known-name race (InQueue), enabling a same-user co-resident process to squat org.rustdesk.rustdesk first; (2) handle_client_message's NewConnection closure discards the dbus_crossroads::Context and performs no sender/caller check, so any same-user process can invoke it directly; (3) core_main.rs's --connect/--password deep-link path embeds the plaintext peer password into uni_links and sends it over this exact unauthenticated channel. All on the per-user SESSION bus (Connection::new_session()) — this is same-UID, same-privilege co-resident IPC abuse, not a privilege-escalation primitive, and the credential-leak sub-case additionally requires winning a login/startup race.
verdict.live_test: On the Linux docker lab: (1) as the same OS user, register a fake `org.rustdesk.rustdesk` service on the session bus with request_name(name, allow_replacement=false, replace_existing=false, do_not_queue=true) before starting rustdesk, confirm rustdesk's own request_name() call returns InQueue (add temporary logging) yet cr.serve() still runs; (2) from a second terminal as the same user run `rustdesk --connect <id> --password <secret>` and confirm the fake service receives the NewConnection call with `password=<secret>` in the uni_links string instead of the real GUI; (3) separately confirm `dbus-send --session --dest=org.rustdesk.rustdesk /dbus org.rustdesk.rustdesk.NewConnection string:'rustdesk://connection/ATTACKERID?password=X'` against the real running GUI succeeds with no sender-identity error, proving the spoofed-link sub-case needs no race at all.
verdict.observed_mitigation: None found in the cited functions that blocks the mechanism itself; the only mitigating factor is architectural — this is per-user D-Bus SESSION bus IPC (Connection::new_session(), dbus.rs:57/40), not the system bus, so the attacker gains no privilege beyond what a co-resident same-UID process already has. This downgrades it from a privilege-escalation finding to a same-privilege IPC information-disclosure / spoofing bug.
